questions.question: What are clinicians' biggest pain points with documentation?

seeded.answer: Clinicians' biggest pain point with documentation is the burden it places on their time. [1] Documentation is ranked as the #1 contributor to burnout among physicians, ahead of patient volume and administrative meetings. [1] Physicians report regularly completing documentation after clinic hours, averaging 1.2 hours per day. [1] Clinicians also express frustration with the time it takes to create detailed and accurate documentation, particularly for complex cases with long medication lists. [2]

sources.participants: Participants: 287 — Physician, Nurse Practitioner, Physician Assistant, Registered Nurse

[HIGH] (documentation as burnout driver) Documentation burden ranked as the #1 self-selected contributor to burnout among physicians specifically (52%), ahead of patient volume (31%) and administrative meetings (12%).
[MEDIUM] (after-hours charting) 64% of physician respondents report regularly completing documentation after clinic hours ('pajama time'), averaging a self-reported 1.2 hours/day.

sources.title: Interview — Rheumatologist on Medication Lines in Scribe Drafts
sources.excerpt: [HIGH] (long lists) Many of their patients have long medication lists: disease-modifying drugs, a steroid, supplements, and drugs for other conditions managed by other clinicians. At most visits only one or two of those lines change. In the draft, a line that changed at this visit and a line that was only mentioned while going through the list look the same, and the underline marks only where the scribe was unsure what it heard. To find what changed they read the whole medication section against the orders they placed and the patient's current list. They put a long list at "fifteen lines, give or take" for many of their patients, an informal impression, not a count.

unseeded.answer:
Clinicians' biggest pain point with documentation is the burden it places on their time. [1] Documentation burden was ranked as the #1 contributor to burnout among physicians specifically (52%), ahead of patient volume (31%) and administrative meetings (12%). [1] 64% of physician respondents report regularly completing documentation after clinic hours ('pajama time'), averaging a self-reported 1.2 hours/day. [1]

Clinicians also expressed concerns about the accuracy and completeness of AI-drafted notes. [2] Scribe-drafted notes often capture what was discussed in the visit but leave out the specificity coding depends on: laterality, acute vs. chronic, type or stage (they gave heart failure type and CKD stage as examples), and the "due to" link between two conditions. [2] When it's missing the coder has two options, query the physician or code to the unspecified level, and they said they are doing both more often than with notes physicians typed from their own templates. [2] They noted the July 2025 prototype's mismatches were mostly at the specificity level too, and expect a suggester reading these notes to hit the same wall. [2]

questions.question: Why didn't physicians trust the ambient scribe's draft notes?

seeded.answer: Physicians did not trust the ambient scribe's draft notes because they worried about the accuracy of the order of events in the history. [1] They also expressed concerns about the scribe picking up on things from the conversation that the physician didn't catch at sign-off. [2]

sources.title: Interview — Returning Internal Medicine Physician on Edits and Trust Over Time
sources.participants: Participants: 1 — P09 — Physician, Internal Medicine (physician), returning from 2026-01-13-usability-test-ambient-scribe-ga-release-candidate ×1
sources.excerpt:
Share with the ambient scribe team that, in this physician's account, the order of events in the history is where drafts go wrong without being underlined, because each word is heard clearly.
When drafts are evaluated, check the sequence of events in the history against the visit, not only word accuracy.
If the team wants to know whether review habits change over time, plan a measure for it; one returning participant's account can't show a trend.

sources.title: Interview — Medical Coder on Coding from AI-Drafted Notes
sources.excerpt: [MEDIUM] (trust in AI-drafted notes) Nothing in the signed note shows which sentences the scribe drafted and which the physician typed or edited. When a sentence looks off (e.g., a diagnosis in the assessment that nothing else in the note supports), the coder can't tell whether it's a documentation problem worth a query or something the scribe picked up from the conversation that the physician didn't catch at sign-off. They weren't asking for a marker on the permanent chart, just "something I can see while I'm coding".

sources.title: Interview — Primary Care Physician on Incidental Content in Scribe Drafts
sources.excerpt: Earlier ambient-scribe research looked at what the scribe gets wrong: medication dosages and sound-alike drug names, and whether clinicians trust the draft enough to skim it. Two sessions touched on what the scribe takes in more broadly. In an October 2025 contextual inquiry, a behavioral health clinician said that any AI tool listening to or drafting behavioral health session notes raises consent and 42 CFR Part 2 questions (2025-10-07-contextual-inquiry-behavioral-health-sensitive-notes/session-notes.md:28); the exclusion of that population from the near-term ambient scribe rollout is recorded in the scope-boundaries finding (scope-boundaries-and-workflow-fit.md:72-74). A care coordinator said the visit notes they read since GA are longer and more conversational than the notes clinicians used to type (2026-03-03-interview-care-coordinator-chart-review-scribe-notes/session-notes.md:31). Neither asked the person signing a draft about content the scribe writes down correctly but that doesn't belong in a visit note: small talk, a patient's remarks about other people, side conversations with a family member in the room. This session asked a primary care physician, two months after the January 2026 GA, what of that kind ends up in their drafts and what they remove before they sign.

sources.title: Interview — Primary Care Physician on Incidental Content in Scribe Drafts
sources.excerpt:
Share with the ambient scribe team that the confidence underline doesn't help with incidental content, because that content is usually transcribed accurately; reviewing for it means reading the whole draft.
If anything is designed for this, explore pointing out lines that may not belong in the note rather than removing them, so the clinician makes the call.
Keep this separate from the transcription-confidence work: it is about what belongs in the note, not whether it was heard correctly.

questions.question: What did nurses want from the AI's citations?

seeded.answer: Nurses wanted inline citations to the specific chart text behind each suggestion, not just a black-box draft. [1] They saw this as important for understanding the reasoning behind the AI's suggestions. [1]

sources.title: AI-Assisted Prior Authorization
sources.excerpt:
AI-drafted prior authorization justifications were tested in two rounds (v1, Apr 2025; v2, Nov 2025) with the same utilization review nurse supervisor across both, which mattered for tracking whether fixes actually landed.
v1 surfaced a correctness bug (citing outdated diagnosis codes) serious enough that participants said it would likely cause payer denials — not a UX problem, a data-freshness/model fix. It also surfaced a durable requirement: nurses want inline citations to the specific chart text behind each suggestion ("show your work"), not just a black-box draft.

questions.question: How did Practice Administrators expect the invite step to work?

seeded.answer:
Three out of four Practice Administrators hesitated at the "Invite your team" step because they were unsure when the email was sent [1][2][3]. They didn't want staff emailed before champion training was booked for the practice [1][2][3].

The sources don't say whether Practice Administrators thought the invite also gave staff access, or only sent the email.

sources.title: The Practice Administrator — Compass AI Practice Setup Journey
sources.excerpt:

questions.question: What evidence supports making the calendar step required in onboarding?

seeded.answer: The only evidence for requiring the calendar step is the designer's statement at session setup that "the calendar step is required because the scribe attaches recordings to scheduled encounters" [1][2][3]. No session tested this rationale [1][2][3].

sources.title: Compass AI Practice Setup — Study Topline
sources.excerpt:
Completing Connect calendar in the test is not a result: the moderator let anyone who stopped continue on a sandbox calendar (2026-02-03 :43-45 ).
The calendar step is required because, in the designer's statement at session setup, the scribe attaches recordings to scheduled encounters ( :38 ). That is the designer's stated rationale; no session tested it (finding :42-44 ).

questions.question: What is unresolved about the session timeout?

seeded.answer:
The interaction of the session lock with an in-progress recording was flagged as unresolved in encounter-view 's own notes, sourced from a May 2025 SSO/MFA interview side comment. [1]

Direct observation confirms the practical impact: all 4 shadowed clinicians assumed a locked session had destroyed their draft and restarted dictation from scratch, even though the draft is preserved server-side. [1]

The 2026-02-17 contextual inquiry found that a session lock during active dictation freezes the ambient-scribe widget with no message, and that all 4 shadowed clinicians assumed the draft was lost and started dictating again, although the draft survives server-side [2]

sources.title: Ambient Scribe — Post-GA Refinements
sources.excerpt: Session lock during active dictation currently reads as silent data loss, even though it isn't. The locked state's interaction with an in-progress recording was flagged as unresolved in encounter-view 's own notes, sourced from a May 2025 SSO/MFA interview side comment. Direct observation confirms the practical impact: all 4 shadowed clinicians assumed a locked session had destroyed their draft and restarted dictation from scratch, even though the draft is preserved server-side. IT Security confirmed the 10-minute idle-timeout policy itself is fixed, but an explicit "paused, draft preserved" state is a UI-only fix, not a policy change.

sources.excerpt: The 2026-02-17 contextual inquiry found that a session lock during active dictation freezes the ambient-scribe widget with no message, and that all 4 shadowed clinicians assumed the draft was lost and started dictating again, although the draft survives server-side (2026-02-17-session-lock-during-dictation/session-notes.md:38-41, read with correction-2026-09-27.md in that folder). A recovery flow with an explicit paused, draft-preserved state is designed but has not shipped. That session did not look at exam-room workstations shared by several clinicians. This session asked a primary care nurse practitioner, two months later, what a lock looks like in their visits and how a shared workstation affects it.

sources.excerpt: Session lock during active dictation currently reads as silent data loss, even though it isn't. The locked state's interaction with an in-progress recording was flagged as unresolved in encounter-view 's own notes, sourced from a May 2025 SSO/MFA interview side comment. Direct observation confirms the practical impact: all 4 shadowed clinicians assumed a locked session had destroyed their draft and restarted dictation from scratch, even though the draft is preserved server-side. IT Security confirmed the 10-minute idle-timeout policy itself is fixed, but an explicit "paused, draft preserved" state is a UI-only fix, not a policy change.

sources.title: Interview — Nurse Practitioner on Session Lock and Shared Exam-Room Workstations
sources.excerpt: The 2026-02-17 contextual inquiry found that a session lock during active dictation freezes the ambient-scribe widget with no message, and that all 4 shadowed clinicians assumed the draft was lost and started dictating again, although the draft survives server-side (2026-02-17-session-lock-during-dictation/session-notes.md:38-41, read with correction-2026-09-27.md in that folder). A recovery flow with an explicit paused, draft-preserved state is designed but has not shipped. That session did not look at exam-room workstations shared by several clinicians. This session asked a primary care nurse practitioner, two months later, what a lock looks like in their visits and how a shared workstation affects it.
